subtype: Not arguing with the confused mind [Response]
passage:
Day centre note, Wednesday afternoon.
Mrs Pema Dorji arrived agitated today, insisting she had to get home because her children would be back from school. Her granddaughter Himani, who drops her off, did not tell her that her children are grown. I watched Himani kneel beside the chair and say, "You're worried about them. You were always the one who fed everyone." Mrs Dorji's shoulders came down. Himani opened the photo album with her, said the children were fine, and asked if she would help fold napkins for tea. Within ten minutes she was folding and humming. Earlier this month Himani used to correct her ("Mola, they're forty now"), and it ended in tears on both sides. I have suggested we keep Mrs Dorji's seat by the window and the same afternoon routine every day.
Centre supervisor

qa.q: Where does the supervisor suggest keeping Mrs Dorji's seat?
qa.a: By the window, with the same afternoon routine every day.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she arrived, and what eased it?
qa.a: She was agitated and worried about her children; Himani naming that worry made her shoulders come down.

qa.q: Why did Himani's new approach work better than correcting?
qa.a: It answered the feeling behind the words instead of arguing over facts Mrs Dorji can't hold, and a calm task gave her comfort.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt earlier in the month when correcting led to tears?
qa.a: Himani was probably frustrated and upset, crying along with her grandmother over an argument nobody could win.

grounding: Shows a caregiver who stops correcting a confused grandmother and responds to the feeling behind her words, with reassurance, routine and calm reducing distress.

passage:
Kavitha: Leela, Appa paid the electricity bill twice this month. And he got lost coming back from the temple on Sunday. Same road for 40 years
Leela: Amma says it's just age. He's 71
Kavitha: I thought so too. But he also shouted at the milkman, and Appa never shouts
Leela: yes... he called me by Amma's name on the phone yesterday
Kavitha: I don't want to scare him. But I think a doctor should properly check, not just us guessing
Leela: what if it's something bad
Kavitha: then we'll know early. We can plan, make the house safe, sort the bank papers while he can still tell us what he wants
Leela: ok. I'll take leave on Thursday and come with you
Kavitha: thank you 🙏 I'll call the memory clinic at the hospital tomorrow

qa.q: Where did Appa get lost on Sunday?
qa.a: Coming back from the temple, on the same road for 40 years.

qa.q: What is Leela worried about when Kavitha suggests a doctor?
qa.a: Leela is afraid the answer might be something bad.

qa.q: Why is seeking an early assessment a wise step here?
qa.a: It replaces guessing with real understanding, so the family can plan for safety and papers while Appa can still share his wishes.

qa.q: How might Appa feel about the family's concern?
qa.a: He might feel embarrassed or frightened, which is why Kavitha wants to go gently and not scare him.

grounding: Shows a family noticing memory, judgment and mood changes in a parent and seeking a doctor's assessment early instead of blaming old age.

passage:
"She's been crying since you left for the shop," Nani said, rocking Sangeeta on her hip.
Shalini dropped the bags. "Come, my baby."
Sangeeta flung out her arms and buried her face in Shalini's neck.
"You'll spoil her, always carrying," Nani said, smiling.
"She's been sick two days. She needs this."
Sangeeta's sobs slowed. Soon she was patting Shalini's cheek. "Amma. Mine."
"See? Calm now," Shalini said softly.

qa.q: Where had Shalini gone?
qa.a: She had left for the shop.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when Shalini came back, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt relieved and safe; she flung out her arms, buried her face and her sobs slowed.

qa.q: Is Shalini spoiling Sangeeta by carrying her? Why or why not?
qa.a: No; warm holding after being sick helps a toddler calm down and trust that comfort will come.

qa.q: How does Nani see all the carrying?
qa.a: Nani teases that it spoils her, but she smiles, and she has been rocking Sangeeta on her hip too.

grounding: Shows a toddler seeking to be held for safety and calming quickly once comfort returns, with warm touch shown as care, not spoiling.

subtype: Child seeking cuddles after a bad day [Actor]
passage: At the day-care centre, Santosh had spilled blue paint on the new mat, and the art teacher had spoken sharply. He spent the afternoon silent on the reading rug. When his mother, Uma, came at five and sat on the little bench to sign the register, Santosh walked over without a word and climbed into her lap, face in her dupatta. Uma put the pen down and held him. She didn't ask anything yet. After a long minute he mumbled, "I made the mat blue." "Ah," she said, rocking him. "Tell me on the way home."

qa.q: What did Santosh spill on the new mat?
qa.a: Blue paint.

qa.q: Why did Santosh climb into Uma's lap without a word?
qa.a: He felt upset and ashamed after being scolded, and wanted comfort before talking.

qa.q: What did Uma get right in that moment?
qa.a: She put the pen down and gave the hug first, leaving the questions for later.

qa.q: How might the art teacher see Santosh's silence that afternoon?
qa.a: The teacher might notice the sharp words hurt him and could offer a kind word the next day.

grounding: Shows a young child who was scolded climbing wordlessly into a parent's lap, and the parent accepting the hug first and talking later.

passage: When the bus from the district school dropped Gargi at the Ranipur crossing, Rehana was waiting as always, arms open. Gargi stepped round the hug and fixed her bag strap. "Not here, Ammi. Everyone's looking." Rehana's arms fell. At home Gargi went straight to the roof. Rehana stood at the stove a long time, stirring nothing. That evening she didn't push. She carried two cups of tea up to the roof and sat beside Gargi on the parapet, shoulders not quite touching, watching the goats come home. After a while Gargi leaned her head on her mother's shoulder, just for a moment. Rehana kept very still and said only, "The tea's getting cold."

qa.q: Where did Rehana carry the two cups of tea?
qa.a: Up to the roof.

qa.q: Why did Gargi step round the hug at the bus stop?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and self-conscious with everyone looking, and wanted her own space.

qa.q: What did Rehana do that kept the connection alive?
qa.a: She didn't push, sat beside Gargi with tea, and let Gargi come closer at her own pace.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when her arms fell?
qa.a: She felt hurt and a bit lost, standing at the stove stirring nothing.

grounding: Shows a teenager stiffening at a public hug while still wanting warmth, and a parent respecting her pace by sitting beside her and keeping closeness on offer.

subtype: Homesick and touch-starved in a hostel [Actor]
passage:
Warden's note, girls' hostel, Block C, 12 October.
Sunaina, first year, from Imphal, has been sitting alone in the common room most evenings, phone on her lap, not really watching the TV. Her roommate mentioned that Sunaina cried after a video call with her grandmother and said, "I just miss someone patting my head." Today I asked if she would like to help with the hostel's rescued cat, which needs feeding at seven. She came, and stayed half an hour with the cat curled against her. I also told her about the Tuesday badminton group that Akash from the sports office runs. She went, and came back laughing with two girls from Block A who linked arms with her on the stairs. I'll keep an eye on her through Diwali, when many go home and she won't.

qa.q: What time does the rescued cat need feeding?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's comment about wanting her head patted reveal?
qa.a: She feels lonely and homesick, aching for the everyday touch of family.

qa.q: Which of the warden's steps were healthy ways to meet Sunaina's need?
qa.a: Inviting her to care for the cat and pointing her to the badminton group, where she made friends who link arms with her.

qa.q: How might Sunaina's roommate feel about seeing her cry?
qa.a: The roommate was probably concerned and sad for her, which is why the roommate told the warden.

grounding: Shows a young adult far from family aching for a casual hug, and a pet, sport and new friends meeting some of that need in healthy ways.

passage: The winter I moved to Chandigarh for a remote job, I went nineteen days without any friendly touch. I only noticed because the pharmacist's hand brushed mine while giving me change, and I nearly cried at the counter. I'm Nikita, and I'd always thought of myself as someone who liked being alone. But that month I was restless, sleeping badly, snapping at my own reflection and tearing up at dog-food adverts. I felt silly for wanting a hug so much. Then my old college friend Asif, who lived across town, messaged about a Sunday cycling group. I went. Afterwards eight of us sat on the grass eating chole kulche, knees bumping, and someone clapped me on the back. I also started calling Mummy every night. Nothing magic. But I stopped feeling like a ghost.

qa.q: How many days did Nikita go without any friendly touch?
qa.a: Nineteen days.

qa.q: Why did Nikita nearly cry at the pharmacy counter?
qa.a: Nikita felt lonely and starved of contact, so even a brush of a hand felt overwhelming.

qa.q: Which safe ways did Nikita find to meet the need for contact?
qa.a: Joining Asif's Sunday cycling group, sharing food on the grass with others, and calling Mummy every night.

qa.q: What might Asif have noticed when Nikita joined the cycling group?
qa.a: Asif may have been glad to see an old friend come out and join in, perhaps without knowing how lonely Nikita had been.

grounding: Shows a person living alone growing restless, low and sensitive after weeks without friendly touch, and meeting the need safely through friends, family and community.

passage: The train to Siliguri was delayed three hours, and the platform at Howrah was a wall of noise. Devika had just hung up after hearing her grandfather was in hospital, and her face had gone blank. Dolma put her arms out, then stopped halfway. "Can I hug you? Or is that too much right now?" Devika shook her head. "Not right now. Sorry." "Don't be sorry." Dolma dropped her arms and sat on their suitcase instead, making room. She bought two cups of chai from the vendor, held one out, and kept her shoulder close without touching. For a while they said nothing. Then Devika started talking about her grandfather's garden, and Dolma just listened, nodding, through three more announcements.

qa.q: How long was the train delayed?
qa.a: Three hours.

qa.q: How did Devika seem to feel after the call, and what shows it?
qa.a: She seemed shocked and overwhelmed; her face had gone blank and she didn't want to be touched.

qa.q: How did Dolma show warmth after Devika said no?
qa.a: She accepted it without offence, made room on the suitcase, brought chai, stayed close without touching and listened.

qa.q: What would have changed if Dolma had hugged Devika without asking?
qa.a: Devika might have felt crowded and even more overwhelmed, and less free to say what she needed.

grounding: Shows a caring friend asking before a hug, accepting a no without offence and finding other ways to show warmth on a noisy, delayed platform.

passage:
Monday: Before the school concert, Dolma pulled at her frock. "My tummy has bees in it." Her mummy, Sangeeta, knelt down. "Bees in your tummy? That can be a nervous feeling. Lots of people get it before a show."
Thursday: Dolma came home from the park stomping, cheeks red. "My face is hot!" Sangeeta said, "Hot face and stompy feet. Maybe that's angry?" Dolma nodded hard. "Kusum took my swing."
Saturday: At bedtime Dolma yawned. "My legs are heavy. That's tired, Mummy." Sangeeta smiled. "You're getting good at listening to your body."

qa.q: What did Dolma say was in her tummy before the concert?
qa.a: She said her tummy had bees in it.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when her face was hot on Thursday?
qa.a: She was angry because Kusum took her swing.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta help Dolma understand her body?
qa.a: She named the feeling that matched each body signal, like bees for nervous and a hot face for angry, and asked rather than told.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel when Dolma names "tired" by herself?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and pleased that Dolma is learning to listen to her body.

grounding: Shows a young child linking feelings to body sensations such as butterflies, a hot face and heavy legs, helped by a parent who names the signals.

subtype: Missing hunger or the need for the toilet [Actor]
passage: On the first day of the kite festival in Deesa, Sachin didn't come down from the terrace for five hours. He was winning, cutting two kites and dodging a third. When Jatin bhaiya called him for lunch, he shouted, "Later!" At four he suddenly burst into tears because his string tangled, then kicked the reel, then ran for the toilet, hopping. Jatin found him afterwards on the stairs, shaky and cross. "When did you last eat, or drink, or pee?" Sachin thought. "Breakfast?" Jatin handed him a roti roll and a water bottle. "Next round, every time the temple bell rings, stop. Tummy, throat, bladder. Check, then fly." The next day Sachin checked at every bell, grumbling, and still cut three kites.

qa.q: What signal did Jatin suggest for a body check?
qa.a: Every time the temple bell rings.

qa.q: Why did Sachin burst into tears over a tangled string?
qa.a: He was hungry, thirsty and needed the toilet without noticing, so he felt shaky and cross, and a small problem felt huge.

qa.q: Why is Jatin's bell check a good idea?
qa.a: It builds a quick habit of noticing hunger, thirst and the bladder before they turn urgent and spoil the fun.

qa.q: How might Jatin have felt when Sachin shouted "Later!"?
qa.a: Jatin was probably a bit annoyed but not surprised, and later helped instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a child absorbed in play ignoring hunger, thirst and a full bladder until he falls apart, and a quick regular body check building awareness.
